scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that genuine commitment can bring honest criticism, then argues it just as often breeds blind loyalty; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: We might expect the strongest supporters of an idea to defend it without any doubt at all.
Some people argue that those most deeply committed to an idea or policy are also the most critical of it.
I agree that genuine commitment can lead to honest criticism, but I do not believe this is true of committed people in general.

sections.role: Body 1 — How commitment can bring criticism

sentences.text: First, people who care deeply about an idea often do examine it most closely.
Because they want the idea to succeed, they study its weaknesses in order to improve it.
For example, a devoted scientist may test her own favourite theory harder than anyone else would.
This shows that real commitment can include a genuine willingness to question and refine.
Those who truly love a cause want it to be as strong and as honest as possible.
Such people criticise not to destroy the idea but to make it better.
In this sense, deep commitment and careful criticism can indeed go together.
Second, however, deep commitment just as often makes people less critical, not more.
Strong belief can blind people to the faults of an idea they have fully embraced.
Consider devoted followers of a movement who refuse to admit even its most obvious mistakes.
Such loyalty shows that commitment can silence doubt rather than sharpen it.
People heavily invested in a policy may defend it stubbornly to avoid admitting they were wrong.
The most committed are sometimes the last to see flaws that outsiders notice at once.
Commitment, then, can produce blind loyalty as easily as honest criticism.
In conclusion, deep commitment to an idea can sometimes lead to its sharpest criticism.
But just as often, strong belief blinds people to the faults they refuse to see.
Whether commitment brings criticism or blindness depends on the honesty of the person who holds it.
